items.question: How did the problem of scalable oversight shape your thinking about AI evaluations and motivate GPQA?
items.object: Scalable oversight and the motivation for GPQA
items.answer: For me, it was mostly thinking about this problem of scalable oversight. As models get more capable, it just gets harder to evaluate their capabilities. If we imagine that models are able to complete tasks that take people a long time to complete or require expertise that you don't necessarily have, you need a method for still being confident in their outputs and trusting their outputs. And so thinking about that problem was a lot of motivation actually for GPQA, and was what kind of started, got me started thinking about evaluations.

If we imagine that models are able to complete tasks that take people a long time to complete or require expertise that you don't necessarily have, you need a method for still being confident in their outputs and trusting their outputs. And so thinking about that problem was a lot of motivation actually for GPQA, and was what kind of started, got me started thinking about evaluations.

rubrics.text: The response frames scalable oversight as establishing confidence in model outputs when evaluators lack the expertise needed to perform the tasks themselves.

items.question: Why do you use human completion time as a unified measure of AI progress?
items.object: Human completion time as a unified measure of AI progress
items.answer:
I guess the place to start for us in terms of the motivation for the time horizon work is to have a unified axis that we can measure AI progress on over a very long period of time. So when we started doing the work, we had this very strong belief that GPT-2 is fundamentally, in some really important sense, much worse as an AI than, I guess, at the time it was maybe Sonnet 3.5, I think, the best model out then. The standard approach is producing, creating a set of tasks and then measuring models' accuracy on these tasks. As models get better, they saturate the benchmark. And then you have to create a new benchmark that has harder tasks. This was kind of the standard approach. And I contributed a benchmark, GPQA, to this approach. But the challenge here is that it's really difficult to compare between these qualitatively different benchmarks. So the set of tasks you evaluate GPT-2 on are like LAMBADA, like complete the last word in this text. And tasks that we were having Sonnet 3.5 try and do were kind of like answer simple Python coding questions, or write a short 20-line Python program. And so it's very difficult, at first blush, to say, okay, yeah, how much harder is writing a Python program than finishing the word in this paragraph? It's kind of hard to think about that.

And so I think the key insight of the time horizons work is to use this notion of human time to complete. So how long does the task take a human to do? A human who has a reasonable amount of expertise such that they would plausibly be doing the task in their work or in their day to day. And the idea was we can use this metric to represent the difficulty of the task in some sense. And then we can compare models across a very wide range of capabilities, all the way from GPT-2 now up to Opus 4.6. That's the high level motivation.

items.question: How do you design time horizon benchmark tasks to probe models' ability to generalize beyond their training data?
items.object: Designing time horizon benchmark tasks to test generalization
items.answer:
On the longer end, we have tasks that either require quite a bit of expertise or many steps to complete. So we have machine learning tasks that are train a model in this kind of—that's very weird, such that the code for training this model is not really online. One example is train a masked language model without using the division or exponentiation operators. And so you actually have to be pretty clever about how you set up the architecture to do this. And the hope is that this can help us measure models' ability to generalize beyond their training data.

There are some which are a bit like ARC-AGI, sort of the themed in that they're like, you have some black box that's computing some function, and you know that it's a composition of some set of primitives, and you've gotta figure out what function it is. Or you have some long binary string, and you've gotta figure out what the pattern continuation is, and sort of puzzle type tasks where it's very—you know, some ML type tasks can be basically regurgitating a tutorial on how to build your first ResNet or whatever, just works pretty well. So, yeah, having these weird tasks that are either some kind of unknown object that you need to interact with and figure out what it is, or a task that resembles normal work but has some weird constraints such that you can't just do the standard thing. I don't think all of our tasks hit those criteria. Some of them, you can just do the standard thing, but we generally try to avoid that.

items.question: Why do you regard successful human attempts as more informative than failures when estimating task difficulty?
items.answer: One of the reasons why we filter our baselines to only ones that succeed is success on a task is a lot more information than failure on a task. There are a bunch of reasons why you might fail a task that aren't actually a lot of information about how difficult it is or how much agency is required. For example, maybe we got their expertise wrong. We're doing this job of manually assigning people to tasks that we think they're relevant for, or that they have a lot of relevant expertise for, and maybe someone just happened to never use this particular tool or set of tools that are super important for this task. Then their failure on that task is still some information, but if they succeed on the task, then that is this very objective thing: yes, someone can complete this task in this amount of time. There are also infrastructure reasons why people fail tasks, and incentive reasons. When you have people try and complete tasks, sometimes they'll get bored and want to stop; sometimes they'll be like, “Ah, this is too hard. I don't want to keep doing this.” Sometimes incentives can be tricky to set up well. One situation you can have is where people quit tasks early because they want to maximize the chances of getting more tasks that they succeed on. Typically we pay bonuses for success because we want to incentivize people to succeed, but that can lead to a perverse incentive. Broadly, we just have a lot more uncertainty about failures than we do about successes.

items.question: What do you see as the main challenge in using task messiness to explain AI benchmark performance?
items.object: Task messiness as an evaluation variable
items.answer:
We are broadly really interested in trying to explain as much of the variance in models' successes and failures as we can. The length of task for humans is one metric that explains a decent amount of this variance, but there are definitely other things going on. We're actually currently trying to figure out what other properties of tasks explain their success and failure well. We would love to have something like this. For something like messiness, or a lot of these other kinds of metrics you can think of, to me the biggest issue or challenge is just some kind of subjectivity. People have very different senses of what is a messy versus clean task, depending on your priors about—

One example is I have a colleague who—I think it's fine for me to talk about this—would not rate any of our tasks as being messy at all because they have algorithmic scoring functions, for example. The success or failure is defined by a small surface area or something. The tasks tell you what to do; in the real world, a lot of the challenge is figuring out what the hell you should do in the first place.

I think that's a challenge, but I definitely think—especially with this randomized control trial that we ran recently of developer productivity, where we saw that developers, at least when we measured this, were not sped up by AI systems—trying to understand the gap between benchmark scores and some of these more ecologically valid experiments, what that gap is or what explains that gap, I think we're super interested in.

items.question: How do you interpret the evidence that AI time horizons may now be doubling faster than the original seven-month trend?
items.object: Four-month versus seven-month time-horizon doubling trends
items.answer:
I would love to know the answer to that. I think we still don't really know. A couple things to say: since we released the paper in March, new—one thing it'd be useful to point out for listeners is that this plot where we measure the trend of improvement over time is only using the best model at a given time. That's relevant because a lot of other models have different trade-offs; maybe they have faster inference but they're weaker, and we're just using the models that perform the best.

Since March, frontier models—one thing we look at in the paper, and this is useful to talk about because I think the timeline is useful for understanding how the paper came together: we initially only fit the trend on models from, I think, basically 2024 onwards. The first version of the graph was made by Ben West in December 2024, if my memory is right, and I think this was just using that year's models. With those models, we observed this four-month doubling time in the time horizon. Then we were like, does this trend extend backwards? In the paper we also do these backcasts from this. Then we added in previous models.

All that's to say that to some extent from the start we've seen these two trends. I think this is all kind of BS or something; once you have 10 or 15 data points and you're fitting piecewise linear functions, it's pretty sketchy. I definitely don't want to overclaim, but it does seem like this four-month doubling-time trend from 2024 onwards has continued to hold, or has been a much better predictor than the seven-month doubling time suggested by models going back to 2019. My best guess, with very low confidence, is something like we're just on this four-month trend now, but it's still exponential. It is really hard to distinguish between different kinds of model fits to some extent.

items.question: How do you think inference costs should affect the interpretation of AI time-horizon results?
items.answer: Models will do lots of reasoning and run a bunch of different experiments on these longer tasks. They'll take something like 10 to 50 actions in the environment, but for each action they're doing a bunch of reasoning. Often, depending on the exact agent scaffold, we have models that propose actions and then review them and select the best one. There's a lot going on, and this is still much cheaper than having people do it. I wish I knew the exact numbers on cost. It is more complicated because of caching, but currently this isn't our biggest concern because models are still highly cost-competitive. I totally imagine this changing at some point. Trends in models being able to use test-time compute more effectively—I totally expect for very long tasks this to get expensive, and it to be very important to be measuring the Pareto frontier of cost and success rate. I think we're excited to do work on this as it becomes more relevant.

items.question: Why do you find AI systems taking over AI research a particularly concerning threat model?
items.answer:
The threat model that METR is most concerned about, at least at the moment, is rapid acceleration in AI capabilities, and in fact the rate of progress of AI capabilities, due to AI systems being able to contribute substantially, or the majority of AI progress, at some point in the future. Currently the way you make AI systems better is through a combination of compute, hardware resources, money, data, and talent, labor, right? If it becomes the case that AI systems can replace the labor, the talent part of this, in economic models of progress—in at least some of them, I think they're reasonable, although I'm not an economist—you can see very rapid progress. This just seems broadly scary.

One example is very rapid centralization of power in a single organization that does this kind of recursive self-improvement, and that's concerning for general stability, geopolitical, democracy kinds of reasons. And then your arguments for why the AI system itself is not going to be dangerous might break down. You might not be able to evaluate it effectively, because the system may have a really good understanding of exactly how you're evaluating it. If its goals are different from yours, it might be very easy for it to game your evaluations. Your supervision methods might break down. You're reading its chains of thought, and the model is saying things that seem safe and nice and reasonable, but actually it's doing some hidden reasoning in the background that you can't detect.

You didn't realize this was about to happen because progress was so fast, and because as a lab you were scrambling to get as much compute and make as much progress as you can as quickly as you can. Broadly, one of the big concerns or questions we want to understand is how close are we to this rapid acceleration? Is that even possible? Labor is not the only input to AI progress. You also have compute and data, for example. These things might be highly complementary to labor, such that even if the amount of talent increases by several orders of magnitude because you have all your AI researchers doing this work, you still might be bottlenecked by compute and data. Trying to get some understanding of that, we do some work or think about these economic models to some extent. I think this isn't our chief forte. Epoch has a bunch of great work doing some of this modeling. Folks at Forethought, Will MacAskill and Tom Davidson, have done work on this kind of economic modeling. Understanding how capable AI systems are is a big input to this, and software engineering and ML research capabilities are highly relevant.

items.question: How did the robustness of the time-horizon trend change your view of economic models of AI progress?
items.answer: I view this time horizon trend that we're seeing as something closer to an economic model than an ML benchmark model. The actual inputs to this progress are firms competing to train increasingly better models and putting these resources in, and they have constraints and whatever. I think this was one of the big updates for me. I'm much more interested in economics as a result of seeing this really robust trend, because I was extremely skeptical of putting time on the x-axis in particular. I thought the inputs would just be random decisions by different labs, and there's no way we'd see some robust trend because it just depends on who Jensen happens to like or whatever, for different compute deals. I thought there was no way that could be robust. That was a decent update for me: maybe these extremely abstract economic models actually can be very informative, or maybe there is a deeper systematicity to AI progress even though zoomed in it feels very contingent and arbitrary. This is all very much speculation, just my musings. As an organization, we would definitely be interested in forecasting. There are trade-offs between doing this more abstract modeling and just focusing on nowcasting, like currently how good are AI systems, which is an open question and there is a lot of disagreement about this. Even internally at METR we have disagreement about this. There probably isn't one single answer because it's a complicated question, but I think we're trying to do both to some extent.

items.question: How did METR's developer productivity randomized controlled trial affect your confidence in time-horizon thresholds for accelerating AI research?
items.object: Developer productivity RCT and useful AI time-horizon thresholds
items.answer:
I think this is an open question. I don't think we have nearly as good an answer here yet as we want. We have heuristics, I think. One week of work, like time horizons of 40 hours: I think we're definitely getting a lot more concerned, or it seems at least plausible that you could successfully or efficiently delegate weeks' worth of work to AI systems, and I could totally imagine that speeding up AI progress quite a bit. Same for time horizons that are much longer, but I think we don't really know.

Part of my uncertainty—I probably would have been more confident in something like a week or a few weeks of work as a time horizon that's very useful as some rough heuristic or threshold before this productivity RCT, where we found that people were very miscalibrated on how much AI systems sped them up, developers, software developers in particular, and in fact we saw they were slowed down on average by about 20%. I think the time horizons work and the randomized control trial results probably aren't as in conflict as they might seem at face value, for reasons we could talk about. They definitely did update me more towards broader uncertainty about this interaction between AI systems and people, and maybe we do end up really bottlenecked by things like our ability to specify tasks really clearly, or maybe things like the fact that we're algorithmically scoring models mean we might be overestimating their capabilities to some extent.

items.question: What did you find striking about time-horizon results for general computer-use benchmarks such as OSWorld?
items.object: OSWorld and multimodal computer-use time horizons
items.answer:
The other interesting takeaway I had from that was with respect to more general computer use. These benchmarks—there's this benchmark OSWorld that has a bunch of tasks where you have a browser and need to do these tasks, or you're in an operating system and have to click around and manipulate normal software. The key difference between this and a lot of our tasks is that our tasks are almost entirely text-only. Models are weaker relatively at multimodal tasks, it seems. For those domains, I think they had something like a similar doubling time, but the absolute time horizons were much lower.

They were a couple minutes or something. I thought that was interesting. I'm actually kind of confused about this broadly; I don't really understand what's going on there.

rubrics.text: The response observes that general computer-use benchmarks appeared to have similar time-horizon doubling times despite much lower absolute time horizons than METR's predominantly text-only tasks.

items.question: Where do you lean on the trade-off between isolating individual AI skills and evaluating realistic work?
items.answer:
I think there is a very real trade-off here between the level of granularity of your understanding—if you maximize that, you end up with very simple, formulaic, systematic benchmarks that are probing some particular skill—and on the other end you have this realism-maximization lens. The best popular example of this maybe is SWE-bench or SWE-bench Verified, where these are actual GitHub issues and PRs and tests that you're measuring AI systems against. There's a real trade-off: on one end you get this granular understanding, and on the other it's really easy to interpret what a success or failure means. It's like, yes, it can do this thing in the real world that I understand and have intuitions about. I think there's a real trade-off.

What do I think here? I think it's really hard. Broadly, I feel pretty pessimistic about the granular approach. Maybe this has something to do with the amount of systematicity in neural networks themselves, where they're just inconsistent but are still capable of really impressive things. Maybe you can't get this extremely crisp understanding and you have to aggregate or look more broadly at things that are relevant for your decisions about whether to deploy a system or how safe it is. That's probably the direction I lean in.

items.question: How do you weigh a constant-hazard explanation of AI task failure against the logistic fit used in METR's time-horizon paper?
items.object: Constant-hazard models of AI task failure
items.answer:
If you assume this constant hazard rate, or per time that people spend there's some percentage chance that the AI system is going to make some kind of catastrophic error and ultimately not succeed at the task, then this is also a good predictor of AI system success and failure on our tasks as a function of the length of task for humans. In our paper we used a logistic fit, but assuming a constant hazard rate you would use an exponential fit.

We did explore different fits, and logistic was a better fit. I don't think it's obvious how—or because of this aggregation of maybe different distributions of tasks—I don't think it's obvious how much we should weigh the exact quality of the fit versus priors on simplicity, or “This is a nice model.” I don't know how much to weigh that, but I think stuff like this is very interesting in terms of understanding capabilities. I often feel like getting at something more like the intrinsic number of actions needed to complete a task feels intuitive. I think other folks I've talked to feel like it's a really nice thing that could be useful for understanding this. You can imagine it slotting well with this constant hazard rate model, where for each action that you need to take. But operationalizing this has been tricky. We've done some analysis of this, and it's been difficult to extract really good insights.

items.question: Why are you cautious about using the human market price of a task to predict AI performance?
items.object: Human market prices as a measure of AI task difficulty
items.answer:
Something like that could be reasonable. A reason you might not expect that to work is that AI systems broadly have a different capability profile than people. If it was 1920, or actually let's say 1950 or 1940, right before we had calculators—

If you were doing this math of how long it takes to pay human computers to calculate the product of 10-digit numbers that you need to do for whatever reason, you'd be like, “Yeah, that's an extremely hard task,” and machines are not going to be able to do that task for a long time. But pretty quickly after computers were able to do this very well. Applying this to modern systems, I do basically believe AI systems are way better at tasks that seem to require humans many years of intellectual development and labor to complete. They can do GPQA questions, they can do IMO problems, these sorts of things. I view this as less of the bottleneck. I think I view something more akin to agency, or being sensitive to the messiness factors. That's not to say there aren't other metrics. Maybe this is an argument against expertise or human expertise.

items.question: What are you trying to learn by manually examining model attempts on SWE-bench?
items.answer:
Over the last couple weeks I've been labeling many dozens of attempts of models on SWE-bench with a bunch of different factors to try and understand, for example, how good are our tests in SWE-bench? Are models often implementing correct functionality that isn't captured by the tests because the tests were written for the specific implementation that the human originally wrote? Alternatively, are models often succeeding as judged by the automatic test cases, but they're actually breaking a bunch of other code that isn't tested in the repo, or their solution is just bad in some other ways so we wouldn't actually call that a success?

Broadly, this is one example of this stream of work we've started doing more of over the past few months: trying to understand benchmarks, the science of evals. How can we interpret certain scores on different benchmarks, ones we've made and ones other folks have made?

items.question: What uncertainty about reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards do you most want to investigate?
items.answer: One example of an open question is training models on verifiable, formally verifiable tasks, like passing test cases. People talk about reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. There's a question of how much progress currently is coming from this, and maybe two corollary questions: how much should we expect progress from training this way to generalize to non-verifiable tasks, or tasks that are messier or more qualitative? Alternatively, if improvements from this type of training don't generalize well, how much human data do you need to train models that are good on more qualitative, messier tasks? Trying to get some sense of things like this is something we're interested in. The exact projects that we'll end up doing will depend on specifics.

items.question: How do you think risk evaluation should evolve once AI systems can do AI research very effectively?
items.object: Risk measurement after effective AI research automation
items.answer: There are big open questions to me around how long we'll be able to continue doing this work—not even just from a tractability perspective, but also from a “will it actually be useful?” perspective, in particular for estimating risk. At a certain point, if we're seeing AI systems able to do AI research very effectively, how do we continue estimating risk? Is risk just maximum? Probably not. People are still going to be doing monitoring, and I expect folks to implement basic control methods. Over the past few months we've started doing more work trying to create better metrics for things like monitorability. I don't know; I haven't been working on it, but I think it's very interesting and exciting work.
